header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Time: 15:00 - 15:48 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (PraxisAI Head of ML), Laura Kim (PraxisAI Infra), Evan Brooks (PraxisAI CTO)
summary: POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscale for PraxisAI: define success criteria (latency/throughput/accuracy), baseline workload sizing (avg/peak QPS, tokens per request), benchmark plan, reserved GPU sizing with burst strategy, fallback policies, timeline for a 1-week benchmark and next steps.
topics: Success criteria, workload profile, reserved vs burst capacity, autoscale triggers, fallback models/regions, benchmark metrics and cadence, security doc requests, timeline and commercial ask.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know how busy it is, quick intros. I'm Maya with Redwood, AE.
[00:07] Daniel Ortiz: Daniel, SE on Redwood side, I'll cover the sizing and benchmarks.
[00:11] Ravi Patel: Ravi here, Head of ML at PraxisAI.
[00:14] Laura Kim: Laura, infra.
[00:16] Evan Brooks: Evan, CTO.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Great. Goal for today is to scope the POC: what success looks like, what load you expect, and how we size reserved GPUs + burst/autoscale and fallback behaviors.
[00:30] Ravi Patel: Yeah, high level we run a summarization and personalization service. Typical request is 300 to 800 tokens, P95 latency target is around 300 ms ideally, but we're flexible if cost tradeoffs make sense. Throughput wise our baseline is ~40 QPS but peaks go to 220 QPS during morning sync windows.
[00:50] Laura Kim: Our infra can route traffic to a test VPC, we can put a NAT there, we want to validate private deployment options but for POC hosted/dedicated is fine.
[01:05] Daniel Ortiz: Awesome. Couple clarifying q's: when you say p95 300 ms, is that end-to-end including network? and are you optimizing for wall-clock latency or tail?
[01:15] Ravi Patel: P95 end-to-end, yes. Tail matters — we need to keep p99 under 700 ms else UX complaints.
[01:24] Daniel Ortiz: Ok, that helps. For model, what are you planning to run?
[01:27] Evan Brooks: We want to try open models first — we've been evaluating Llama-3 style variants and a smaller in-house fine tuned model for personalization. We'll also test a quantized 4-bit variant for cost.
[01:40] Maya Chen: Perfect, so typical POC flow: we'll provision reserved GPUs for steady-state capacity, add burst pool for spikes, and set autoscale triggers to spin up additional capacity before latency SLO breaks. Also fallback policies to smaller models or region failover.
[01:55] Laura Kim: For reserved, are we talking a full node reserve or fractional? We want predictable billing.
[02:02] Daniel Ortiz: Redwood Dedicated supports fractional reservation by vGPU or full node depending on infra. For the POC we usually recommend reserving enough capacity for baseline plus ~25% buffer, and configure burst for peak delta. Example: if baseline 40 QPS maps to 2x A100-equivalents, we reserve 2 and set burst up to 6 for peak 220 QPS depending on batching.
[02:24] Ravi Patel: How do you map QPS to GPUs? Our requests are variable tokens though.
[02:27] Daniel Ortiz: Right, we do a tokens-per-second model. We'll run a quick benchmark with your prompt set to measure tokens/sec per GPU at target latency. Then we'll estimate required GPU count for baseline and peak. For rough math: if one GPU can handle ~60 tokens/sec at p95 300ms for your model, and average tokens per req is 500, that's 0.12 req/sec per GPU — so that's not ideal. But with batching and sequence caching for repeated contexts, effective throughput improves. This is why we need the benchmark numbers.
[03:00] Evan Brooks: Caching could help — most of our requests share user history prefixes.
[03:05] Daniel Ortiz: Exactly, KV cache and prefix reuse can cut token work. We'll instrument the test to measure effective reuse.
[03:12] Maya Chen: On fallback policies: typical patterns we set are fallback to a smaller model first (e.g., 7B quantized) when latency climbs, then region fallback or queueing with graceful degradation. Does that align with your tolerance?
[03:26] Ravi Patel: Yes, fallback to cheaper model is fine as long as we flag quality changes to the app. We can accept slight degradation for short windows.
[03:34] Laura Kim: On security, we'll need SOC2 docs and details on KMS integrations, and audit logs for requests.
[03:40] Maya Chen: We'll share SOC2, the KMS/HSM integration notes, and our audit/logging schema. Daniel — can you drop the docs link?
[03:46] Daniel Ortiz: Yep, I'll include them in the follow-up.
[03:48] Maya Chen: Great. Timeline — we typically run a 1-week benchmark in a dedicated environment: 2 days of baseline warmup, 3 full days of steady and peak tests, final 2 days for failover and regression tests. So about 7-10 calendar days from provisioning. Does that work?
[04:05] Ravi Patel: That sounds good. We want results and a cost estimate to evaluate reserved vs burst.
[04:11] Daniel Ortiz: For sizing proposal we'll provide two capacity plans: conservative (reserve capacity for baseline + 25%) and aggressive (reserve for baseline + burst capacity for common peaks) with cost delta and suggested autoscale thresholds.
[04:24] Evan Brooks: Can you explain the autoscale triggers in more detail? How fast can it spin up GPUs and what's the warm-up?
[04:31] Daniel Ortiz: Good q. Autoscale reaction time depends on infra — for cloud-backed Dedicated, we can spin up pre-warmed instances within 90-180s if images are cached; for on-prem it can be longer. To minimize cold starts we use a warm pool (hot standbys) and kernel-level fast path. For the POC we recommend keeping 1-2 hot nodes for quick bursts and let autoscale add then scale back.
[04:55] Laura Kim: Warm pool costs more; we need clear cost numbers vs risk.
[04:59] Daniel Ortiz: We'll calculate cost per hour for reserved, warm pool, and on-demand burst in the proposal.
[05:05] Ravi Patel: What's the fallback ordering you'd recommend? Smaller quantized model -> queueing -> region fallback?
[05:13] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, that's common. Also one policy is degrade by response length (truncate or synthesize shorter outputs) as an intermediate step. We'll include those policy options in the POC config.
[05:24] Maya Chen: Success criteria — let's get explicit. Ravi, what would make the POC a success for you?
[05:29] Ravi Patel: Three things: 1) p95 latency under 300-350ms under baseline load (40 QPS) and p99 < 700ms; 2) cost per 1M tokens within X (we'll define target after your cost numbers); 3) no data leakage and audit logs present. Also smooth autoscale during a 5x spike without >20% error rate.
[05:51] Maya Chen: We'll map that to test suites. We'll capture p95/p99, error rates, model degradation detection, and autoscale effectiveness.
[05:58] Daniel Ortiz: For benchmarks we'll need your real prompt set and a synthetic peak schedule. If you can provide expected QPS time-series and a 1000-sample prompt corpus that shows token distribution that would be ideal.
[06:10] Laura Kim: Laura will send QPS history and a scrubbed prompt sample.
[06:14] Maya Chen: Perfect. Commercials — POC billing options: 1) short-term reserved commitment for baseline capacity (monthly pro-rata), 2) fully on-demand with higher unit costs, or 3) reserved + burst (recommended). We'll outline costs in the proposal.
[06:29] Ravi Patel: Do you have an SLA for POCs?
[06:31] Maya Chen: We offer standard test-time support; production SLAs are part of Dedicated contracts. For POC we provide monitoring dashboards and SE support for the benchmark window.
[06:41] Evan Brooks: Regarding metrics, we also want token-level cost breakdown and per-request tracing to link user incidents to model runs.
[06:48] Daniel Ortiz: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and tracing. We'll provide a link to a demo dashboard.
[06:53] Laura Kim: Network egress cost — if we run in a cloud region we need estimates.
[06:58] Daniel Ortiz: We'll include region-specific egress and instance cost in the proposal, and call out if private on-prem option is significantly different.
[07:05] Maya Chen: Ok, on the POC plan deliverables: proposal + pricing, benchmark plan + harness, security docs, and a calendar for provisioning and benchmark week. We'll aim to get the proposal to you by 2026-07-11.
[07:18] Ravi Patel: Good. One more: can you test model quantization and show accuracy delta vs latency/cost?
[07:24] Daniel Ortiz: Yes — we'll include A/B runs: FP16, 8-bit, and 4-bit quantized runs and report quality regressions on your evaluation prompts.
[07:33] Evan Brooks: Any limitations on model sizes we can run in POC?
[07:36] Daniel Ortiz: We support a wide range; very large models require more GPUs and different kernel optimizations which we'll call out. For POC we'll prioritize models you actually plan to ship.
[07:46] Maya Chen: Alright, let's recap next steps and owners.
[07:49] Maya Chen: Maya to send formal POC proposal + pricing (due 2026-07-11).
[07:54] Daniel Ortiz: I'll send benchmark plan, harness link, and the docs bundle by 2026-07-13.
[07:59] Laura Kim: I'll send the QPS history and scrubbed prompt corpus by 2026-07-12.
[08:04] Ravi Patel: We'll confirm the week for the benchmark — tentatively 2026-07-20.
[08:08] Evan Brooks: Thanks team, looking forward to the numbers.
[08:11] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the attachments and a calendar invite.
[48:00] -- meeting end --

Notes: transcription contains minor mis-hears, product names referenced as "Redwood Dedicated" and sometimes truncated as "Redwood Dedicate" in audio. Some technical terms spelled phonetically (KV cache as "K-V cash").
